correctness.rationale: For a substring of length ell starting at residue r, the number of increasing wrap transitions is floor((r+ell-1)/q), and its greedy subsequence embedding in the opposite increasing-period source uses one new period per other (descending) adjacent pair. Thus embedding is equivalent to ell-1-wraps<=m-1. Optimizing the wrap count gives min(n-1,ceil((ell-1)/q)), yielding the three exact length bounds; intersecting the residue inequalities lists every optimal distinct factor and counts them. The proof treats ell=1, n=1, all endpoints and every q>=2,m,n>=1. Direct enumeration independently checked 567 full parameter triples and 70,756 factor cells. Neither finite enumeration nor any old analysis is used as an infinite certificate.

broader_coverage.reasoning: General exact LCSS algorithms logically compute each finite pair but give neither a closed expression in the three free integer parameters nor all distinct optimal words. The older LCS result about opposite periodic words concerns scattered embeddings in both words; a LCS bound alone does not determine which of them are a contiguous factor of the other word. In the balanced q=3,m=n=4 example, the hybrid optimum is 6 while an ordinary common subsequence has length at least 7.

value.rationale: The 2026 LCSS complexity analysis motivates structured classes of the asymmetric subsequence-substring objective. Opposite periodic permutations are a canonical maximal-order-conflict input family; the theorem gives its exact optimum and all attaining distinct factors, and proves a linear separation from ordinary LCS for any fixed alphabet size at least three. This is an exact natural infinite classification, not an arbitrary parameter slice, routine code output, or claim about general LCSS complexity.
